sections.heading: Newton's three laws of motion
sections.specBullet: Newton's laws of motion applied to sporting movement

rows: Newton's first law (inertia)

A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless an external force acts upon it. A force is required to change a body's state of motion: starting, stopping, accelerating, decelerating or changing direction
A stationary ball stays still until a player applies a force to it
Newton's second law (acceleration)
The acceleration of a body is proportional to the force causing it, and takes place in the direction that force acts
The harder a ball is kicked, the greater its acceleration, so it travels further and faster in the direction the force was applied
Newton's third law (action and reaction)
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When one body exerts a force on another, the second body exerts an equal and opposite force back
A player jumping to win a header pushes down on the ground, and the ground pushes back up with an equal and opposite force, producing the jump

blocks.meaning: For a given mass, acceleration is directly proportional to the force applied.

items.meaning: The resistance a body has to a change in its state of motion. It increases with mass, so a heavier object needs a larger force to change its motion. A heavier rugby forward is harder to stop running than a lighter winger.

The equal and opposite force the ground exerts back on a performer who applies a muscular force against it. A sprinter pushes back on the blocks and the blocks push the athlete forward; a swimmer pushes back against the water and is propelled forward by it.

paragraphs: A high jumper shows the first law directly: they move horizontally at a constant state until take-off, where an external force changes their motion to vertical to clear the bar.

Where that force originates is the second law's business. Coming out of the blocks, a sprinter generates it internally, through the gluteals, quadriceps and gastrocnemius. A tennis player does it through the racket, and the ball leaves accelerating along whatever line the force was applied.

sections.heading: Measurements used in linear motion
sections.specBullet: Scalar quantities: distance and speed

items.meaning: Describes only the size or magnitude of a measurement, with no direction taken into account. Speed and distance are both scalar quantities.
The total length of the path a body follows moving from one point to another. A completed 200m race covers a distance of 200m.
The rate of change of position.

blocks.meaning: The units must be matched: distance in kilometres and time in hours gives speed in km/h.

paragraphs: On a distance against time graph, a horizontal line shows a stationary performer, and a straight, angled line shows constant speed. The steeper the line, the greater the speed.

sections.heading: Centre of mass and the line of gravity
sections.specBullet: Centre of mass and line of gravity

items.meaning: A body's point of balance, where its mass is concentrated. Because the human body is an irregular, constantly moving shape, its centre of mass shifts continuously. Raising the arms overhead raises the centre of mass to help maintain balance.
The vertical line running straight down from the centre of mass to the ground.

paragraphs: In a standing position the centre of mass sits roughly around the hip region, and it differs by gender: typically slightly higher in males, who carry more upper-body mass, and slightly lower in females, where more mass is concentrated at the hips.

sections.heading: Factors affecting stability
sections.specBullet: The factors affecting balance and stability

paragraphs: Good balance and stability matter in almost every sporting action, since an unbalanced kick or tackle is far less effective. Four mechanical factors decide how stable a performer is.

items.term: Height of the centre of mass
items.meaning: A lower centre of mass increases stability. A low stance in rugby, judo or wrestling makes a performer harder to push over.

items.term: Position of the line of gravity
items.meaning: Stability is greatest when the line of gravity falls centrally over the base of support. Moving the centre of mass towards the edge of the base causes over-balancing, which sprinters use deliberately in the blocks to generate forward momentum off the gun.

items.term: Area of the base of support
items.meaning: More contact points create a larger base and greater stability. A headstand, with more contact points, is more stable than a handstand.
Greater mass generally increases stability, through greater inertia.

paragraphs: These principles get used strategically. The Fosbury flop lets a high jumper's centre of mass pass under the bar while the body passes over it, so less height has to be gained overall. In older techniques such as the scissor kick, the centre of mass stays inside the body and has to be lifted fully over the bar.

sections.heading: Lever components
sections.specBullet: The components of a lever system

items.meaning: A rigid rod, in the body a bone, that rotates about a fixed point when a force is applied. Levers let the body produce and control movement efficiently.
The fixed point about which the lever rotates. In the body this is a joint.
The force applied to move the lever. In the body this is the muscular force generated by a contracting muscle.
The weight being moved by the lever, made up of the weight of the body part itself plus anything else being moved, such as a held object.

sections.heading: The three classes of lever
sections.specBullet: First, second and third-class levers

rows: First-class lever
The fulcrum sits between the effort and the resistance: R-F-E or E-F-R

The triceps brachii extending the elbow. The elbow joint is the fulcrum, between the effort of the triceps pulling on the forearm and the resistance of the forearm and hand's weight. Also at the neck: nodding the head forward and back uses the atlanto-occipital joint as the fulcrum, with the neck extensor muscles providing effort against the resistance of the head's weight
Second-class lever
The resistance sits between the fulcrum and the effort: F-R-E. The rarest type found in the human body.

Standing up onto tip-toes, or plantarflexion. The ball of the foot is the fulcrum, the body weight pushing down through the ankle is the resistance, and the effort comes from the gastrocnemius pulling up on the heel via the Achilles tendon
Third-class lever
The effort sits between the fulcrum and the resistance: F-E-R. By far the most common arrangement in the human body.

Flexing the elbow using the biceps brachii. The elbow joint is the fulcrum, the biceps inserting on the radius provides the effort, and the hand or any weight held in it is the resistance, positioned further from the fulcrum than the effort. The hamstrings flexing the knee and the hip flexors flexing the hip follow the same pattern

intro: Take the parts in the order fulcrum, load, effort. The class number tells you which one sits in the middle, and the other two sit either side.
The tables above call the load the resistance, so F, L, E and F, R, E are the same order.
items: 1st class: fulcrum in the middle, load and effort either side
2nd class: load in the middle, fulcrum and effort either side
3rd class: effort in the middle, fulcrum and load either side
In the table above: triceps at the elbow is 1st, rising onto tip-toes is 2nd, the biceps curl is 3rd
Third class is most common, second class is rarest
Name the three components first, then work out which one sits in the middle

sections.heading: Mechanical advantage and disadvantage
sections.specBullet: Mechanical advantage and mechanical disadvantage

items.meaning: The distance between the fulcrum and the point where effort is applied.
The distance between the fulcrum and the resistance.
Where the force arm is longer than the resistance arm. A relatively small effort can move a large resistance, though the resistance moves only a short distance and relatively slowly.

Where the resistance arm is longer than the force arm. A relatively large effort is needed to move even a small resistance, but in exchange the resistance moves a greater distance and at greater speed.

columns: What that gives, and what it costs
rows: First-class lever
Mechanical disadvantage, in the elbow extension example
A large range of movement, and the resistance can be moved quickly, but little force can be applied to it
Second-class lever
Mechanical advantage
Much larger forces can be generated, enough to lift the whole body weight in plantarflexion, but the movement is slow and the range of movement is limited
Third-class lever
Mechanical disadvantage
A large range of movement, and the resistance can be moved quickly, but little force can be applied to it

paragraphs: Comparing the two arm lengths is what determines how efficiently a lever operates. Most third-class levers in the body, the most common type, operate at a mechanical disadvantage, because the effort acts closer to the fulcrum than the resistance does.

That is a trade-off the body makes deliberately. It sacrifices force for a large gain in speed and range of movement at the end of the limb, which is exactly what fast, powerful actions such as kicking and throwing need.

sections.heading: Mass and weight
sections.specBullet: Mass, weight, scalar and vector quantities

items.meaning: A measurement where only size matters, with no direction taken into account.
A measurement that states both size and direction.

The amount of matter, meaning muscle, bone, fat and fluid, that makes up a body, measured in kilograms. It is a scalar quantity and does not change with location. A rugby prop has far greater mass than a gymnast.
A vector quantity: the gravitational force pulling a body towards the centre of the Earth.

blocks.meaning: Gravitational strength is constant across the Earth's surface, so a performer with greater mass has correspondingly greater weight.

paragraphs: An object's mass stays fixed wherever it is, but its weight would change on a planet or moon with different gravity. On the moon an object weighs roughly a sixth of what it weighs on Earth, despite having identical mass in both places.

sections.heading: Distance and displacement
sections.specBullet: Distance and displacement

items.meaning: A scalar quantity: the total length of the path covered between a start and a finish point, regardless of the route taken. One full lap of a 200m track covers a distance of 200m.

A vector quantity: the straight-line distance and direction from start to finish. In a full lap of a track, displacement is zero, because the performer finishes where they started, even though the distance covered was 200m.

paragraphs: The difference shows up most clearly in curved paths. A javelin throw and a basketball free throw both follow a curved flight path, which is the greater distance travelled, while their displacement is the straight line from release point to landing or to the basket.

sections.heading: Speed and velocity
sections.specBullet: Speed and velocity

items.meaning: A scalar quantity measuring how fast a body is moving, with no direction specified.
A vector quantity measuring how fast a body is moving, and in which direction.

blocks.meaning: How far was covered, divided by how long it took.
The same calculation using displacement instead of distance, which is what adds direction.

paragraphs: Velocity gives a more complete picture of motion than speed, because it also states the direction the performer or object is moving in.

sections.heading: Distance-time graphs
sections.specBullet: Interpreting distance-time graphs

items.meaning: Plots the total distance a performer has covered against time. The shape of the line reveals how their motion has changed.

rows: Flat horizontal section
The performer is stationary, since no further distance is being covered as time passes
Straight diagonal line
Constant speed. The steeper the gradient, the greater that constant speed
Curve getting progressively steeper
Acceleration: more distance is covered in each successive time period, as when building up speed from a standing start
Curve flattening out
Deceleration: less distance is covered in each period, as near the end of a run

blocks.title: One 20 second run, plotted as distance against time
blocks.caption: The gradient is the speed. It steepens while the runner builds up speed, holds straight while that speed is constant, flattens as they slow, and is level once they stop. Plotted as velocity, the same run looks like the graph below.

sections.heading: Velocity-time graphs
sections.specBullet: Interpreting velocity-time graphs

items.meaning: Plots velocity against time. Its gradient, the change in velocity divided by the change in time, reveals the performer's acceleration at any point.

rows: Flat horizontal line
Constant velocity, since the gradient, and therefore acceleration, is zero
Constant positive gradient
Constant, or uniform, acceleration
Curve getting progressively steeper
Increasing acceleration: velocity is rising by a greater amount in each successive time period
Downward-sloping section
The performer is decelerating
Line crossing below the time axis
The body has reversed direction. Velocity is a vector, so a negative value means motion is now happening the opposite way

blocks.title: The same run, plotted as velocity against time
blocks.caption: Here the gradient is the acceleration. The rising line is uniform acceleration, the flat section is zero acceleration rather than zero speed, and the falling line is deceleration.

sections.heading: Acceleration
sections.specBullet: Acceleration and deceleration

items.meaning: The rate of change of velocity, measured in metres per second squared. It is a vector quantity. A rise in velocity is a positive acceleration; a fall in velocity is a negative acceleration, or deceleration.

blocks.meaning: How much the velocity changed, divided by how long the change took.

paragraphs: This gets applied to split-time data, such as comparing a sprinter's velocity across consecutive ten-metre sections of a race, to see where they were accelerating most and where their acceleration had levelled off.

sections.heading: Momentum
sections.specBullet: Momentum and its conservation

items.meaning: The quantity of motion a moving body possesses. Because it is calculated using velocity, momentum is itself a vector quantity.

blocks.meaning: Increase either the mass or the velocity and momentum goes up.

paragraphs: Because momentum depends on both factors, a heavier player moving at the same speed as a lighter one generates more momentum, and is therefore harder to stop or to turn. A prop forward and a winger running at the same pace are not equally easy to tackle.

Momentum is conserved when no external force acts on a body or object in flight. It stays the same unless something, such as gravity, air resistance or contact with another body, changes its velocity.

sections.heading: Internal and external forces
sections.specBullet: Internal and external forces

items.meaning: What is required to change a body's state of motion.
Produced by the body's own skeletal muscles contracting, such as the quadriceps concentrically contracting to extend the knee when jumping.
Originates from outside the body: friction, air resistance or gravity.

paragraphs: The two work together. Internal muscular force lets a runner generate the force needed to move, while external forces such as friction and air resistance act to resist that movement.

sections.heading: Vertical forces: weight and reaction
sections.specBullet: Vertical forces acting on a performer

items.meaning: Acts as a vertical force pulling a performer down towards the ground, equal to mass multiplied by the acceleration due to gravity.
Occurs whenever two bodies are in contact, following Newton's third law: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force.

paragraphs: A boot striking a ball drives force forward and downward into it, and the ball pushes back into the boot just as hard, in the opposite direction. Every running stride is the same exchange. The foot presses into the ground, the ground presses back with equal force, and that returned force is what drives the runner forward.

sections.heading: Horizontal forces: friction and air resistance
sections.specBullet: Friction and air resistance

items.meaning: Occurs whenever two surfaces in contact tend to slip or slide against one another. It always acts in the opposite direction to that slipping motion. For a sprinter the foot tends to slip backward on push-off, so the friction arrow acting on the foot points forward.
A form of drag that opposes a body's motion as it travels through air.

rows: Factor one
The surface characteristics of the two bodies in contact. Rougher surfaces, such as spiked running shoes, increase friction and grip
The velocity of the moving body. Faster movement meets greater resistance
Factor two
The temperature of the two surfaces. Sweeping the ice ahead of a curling stone slightly warms its surface, reducing friction so the stone travels further
The cross-sectional area presented to the air. An upright cyclist meets more air resistance than one crouched low over the handlebars
Factor three
The mass of the object sliding. A larger mass increases friction
The shape and surface of the body. Smooth, streamlined shapes, such as a swimmer's shaved body and streamlined cap, reduce resistance compared with a rougher profile

sections.heading: Free body diagrams and net force
sections.specBullet: Free body diagrams and net force

items.meaning: Represents the forces acting on a performer at a single instant using arrows. The arrow's length shows the size of the force, its starting point shows where it is applied, and its direction shows the direction the force acts in.
What remains once all the forces acting on a body have been combined.

paragraphs: Where two opposing forces match, they cancel out: net force comes to zero, nothing about the motion changes, and the body is balanced. Where one outweighs the other, the leftover is an unbalanced force and the motion changes to match it. That is why a jumper rises once reaction force beats bodyweight, and why a sprinter accelerates once propulsive friction beats the resistance working against them.

In events combining vertical and horizontal force, the ratio between the two components of the resultant force shapes the outcome. A high jumper's technique emphasises a large vertical component to maximise height, whereas a long jumper emphasises a larger horizontal component relative to the vertical, to maximise distance.

sections.heading: Impulse and force-time graphs
sections.specBullet: Impulse and the interpretation of force-time graphs

items.meaning: The amount of time a force is applied for.

blocks.meaning: A change in momentum needs a force applied over time, so increasing impulse increases the change in momentum.

rows: Increase momentum
Extend the time the force acts for, or increase the force applied

A basketball player extending their arms and legs through a jump to generate a larger vertical impulse and jump higher; a hammer thrower using several full turns to apply force over a longer time and build greater release speed
Decrease momentum safely
Extend the time over which a force is absorbed
A gymnast bending the hips, knees and ankles on landing from the parallel bars, spreading the impact over more time and reducing injury risk, rather than landing stiffly

items.meaning: Shows how the force applied to the ground changes across a movement. The area under the curve represents impulse.

The positive and negative portions of a force-time graph combined. In sprinting, a large positive impulse occurs as the foot drives into the ground and the reaction force accelerates the athlete forward, while a smaller negative impulse occurs as the foot lands and briefly decelerates the body.

rows: Early in the race
Positive impulse dominates
Acceleration
Mid-race
Positive and negative impulses roughly balance
Constant velocity
Towards the end, as the athlete tires
Negative impulse can begin to dominate
Deceleration

sections.heading: Angular motion and eccentric force
sections.specBullet: Angular motion and the eccentric force that produces it

items.meaning: Movement or rotation around a fixed point or axis. It can be whole-body rotation, such as a somersault, or rotation of individual body parts around a joint, such as the arm rotating at the shoulder when bowling in cricket.

A force applied away from an object's centre of mass, which causes it to turn rather than travel in a straight line. A force applied directly through the centre of mass, a concentric force, produces pure linear motion with no rotation.

paragraphs: Even sports that look purely linear contain a large angular component. In sprinting the arms and legs rotate continuously around the shoulder and hip joints while the athlete travels forward in a straight line.

sections.heading: Axes of rotation
sections.specBullet: The three axes of rotation

rows: Transverse axis
Side to side through the body
A forward or backward somersault
Sagittal axis
Front to back through the body
A cartwheel
Longitudinal axis
Top to bottom through the body
A spin in figure skating

paragraphs: Which axis the body rotates around depends on the direction of the eccentric force applied.

sections.heading: Torque
sections.specBullet: Torque, or the moment of a force

items.meaning: Also called a moment. The rotational effect of a force, the turning effect that causes a body to rotate about its axis.

blocks.equation: Torque (newton metres) = Force (newtons) × Perpendicular distance from the fulcrum (metres)
blocks.meaning: Increase the force, or apply the same force further from the axis, and torque goes up.

paragraphs: A longer moment arm is why pushing a door open near its hinge takes far more force than pushing the same door at its outer edge. The perpendicular distance from the pivot is far greater at the edge.

sections.heading: Newton's laws applied to angular motion
sections.specBullet: Newton's laws of motion applied to rotation

paragraphs: The three laws carry over to rotational movement by substituting torque for force, and angular momentum for momentum.

rows: Newton's first law (angular)
A rotating body continues to spin about its axis with constant angular momentum unless an external torque acts upon it
An ice skater performing a jump keeps spinning at a constant rate throughout the flight phase. Only the torque generated when the skates strike the ice changes their rotational motion
Newton's second law (angular)
The rate of change of a body's angular momentum is proportional to the torque causing it, and takes place in the direction that torque acts
A larger torque produces a faster rotation
Newton's third law (angular)
For every torque applied by one body to another, an equal and opposite torque is exerted back
A goalkeeper throwing both arms upward to tip a shot over the bar generates an equal and opposite reaction that swings their lower legs backward

sections.heading: Angular displacement, velocity and acceleration
sections.specBullet: Angular displacement, angular velocity and angular acceleration

items.meaning: The smallest angle of turn between a body's starting and finishing position during a rotation, measured in degrees or in radians.
The unit angular displacement is often measured in. One radian is 57.3 degrees.
A vector quantity describing rotational speed together with the axis being rotated around.
The rate of change of angular velocity.

blocks.equation: Angular velocity (rad/s) = Angular displacement (rad) ÷ Time taken (s)
blocks.meaning: How far the body turned, divided by how long the turn took.

blocks.equation: Angular acceleration (rad/s²) = Change in angular velocity (rad/s) ÷ Time taken (s)
blocks.meaning: How much the rotational speed changed, divided by the time the change took.

sections.heading: Moment of inertia
sections.specBullet: Moment of inertia and the factors affecting it

items.meaning: A body's resistance to angular motion: resistance both to starting a rotation and, once rotating, to having that rotation stopped. A revolving door is hard to get moving and then equally hard to bring to a stop.
Greater mass increases moment of inertia and therefore resistance to rotation. A bowling ball is harder to start rolling than a football, but equally harder to stop once moving.

items.term: Distribution of mass relative to the axis of rotation
items.meaning: The further a body's mass is spread from its axis of rotation, the greater its moment of inertia.

paragraphs: That second factor is why an open, straight-body somersault, where the diver's mass is extended away from the axis, has a higher moment of inertia and is harder to perform than a tucked somersault, where the mass is pulled in close to the axis.

The same principle operates inside a single sprinting stride. The recovery leg is drawn in with a high knee lift, which brings its mass closer to the hip joint and lowers its moment of inertia, so it can swing through faster ready for the next drive phase.

sections.heading: Angular momentum and its conservation
sections.specBullet: Angular momentum and the conservation of angular momentum

items.meaning: The quantity of rotation, or spin, a body possesses.

blocks.equation: Angular momentum = Moment of inertia × Angular velocity
blocks.meaning: Moment of inertia and angular velocity are inversely proportional: if one increases, the other must decrease to keep angular momentum unchanged.

paragraphs: Angular momentum is conserved, meaning it stays constant, whenever no external torque acts on a rotating body. That applies during flight, and on very low-friction surfaces such as ice. Once a diver leaves the board their overall angular momentum is fixed for the whole dive, and can only change again through an external torque such as hitting the water.

rows: A figure skater starts a spin with arms and one leg extended outward
Large
Slower rotation
The skater pulls the limbs in tight to the body
Small
Sharply increased, producing a much faster spin
A diver extends out of a tuck just before entering the water
Increased
Slowed, which helps them straighten out and control the entry

items: Angular momentum is fixed in flight, so only moment of inertia can be changed
Mass in close means a low moment of inertia and a fast spin
Mass spread out means a high moment of inertia and a slow spin

sections.heading: Projectile motion
sections.specBullet: What makes a body a projectile

items.meaning: The flight of an object, or of the human body, once it is travelling through the air and no longer in contact with the ground or another surface providing force.

paragraphs: The instant contact ends, a ball is a projectile: kicked, thrown or struck, it is on its own from that point. Bodies behave no differently. A long jumper, a high jumper or a gymnast on the vault becomes a projectile the moment their feet leave the ground.

sections.heading: Angle of release
sections.specBullet: The angle of release and its optimum value

items.meaning: The angle between the horizontal and the direction the projectile is travelling at the moment it is released.
The straight-line horizontal distance covered from release to landing. Three factors determine it: angle, speed and height of release.
The release angle producing maximum horizontal distance. It depends on how release height compares with landing height.

columns: Release height compared with landing height
rows: Equal
45 degrees, ignoring air resistance
A long jumper, who takes off from and lands on the same level ground
Lower than landing height
Greater than 45 degrees
Shooting a basketball, where the ball is released below the height of the ring
Higher than landing height
Less than 45 degrees
The shot put, where the athlete releases from hand height, well above the ground where it lands

paragraphs: In practice elite shot putters typically use a release angle of around 26 to 38 degrees, because a lower angle allows greater release speed to be generated. The ideal angle for any individual also depends on their size, strength and technique.

sections.heading: Speed and height of release
sections.specBullet: Speed of release and height of release

items.meaning: A greater speed of release increases horizontal displacement. In the shot put, the speed generated by the athlete's shift or rotation across the circle determines how fast the shot leaves the hand, and a faster release travels further.

A greater height of release also increases horizontal displacement, because gravity acts on the projectile for a longer overall flight, giving it more time and space to travel horizontally before landing.

paragraphs: A taller cricket fielder throwing from a greater height will, all else being equal, achieve greater horizontal distance than a shorter fielder using the same release angle and speed. The shorter fielder would have to alter either their angle or their speed of release to match that distance.

sections.heading: Parabolic and non-parabolic flight paths
sections.specBullet: Parabolic and distorted flight paths

paragraphs: Once in the air, a projectile's flight path is shaped by two opposing forces: its weight, pulling it down under gravity, and air resistance, opposing its motion through the air. Which of the two dominates decides the shape of the path.

rows: True parabolic flight path
Where the projectile has a large weight relative to a small air resistance force. A parabola is a smooth, symmetrical curve
A shot put, which is heavy and compact, so weight dominates over the comparatively small air resistance acting on it throughout flight
Distorted (non-parabolic) flight path
Where the projectile is lighter, or has an irregular shape that increases drag, so air resistance affects it more heavily
A badminton shuttlecock, which starts a serve at high velocity from the racket but slows rapidly and loses its symmetrical curve as air resistance comes to dominate its very light weight

paragraphs: Time in the air matters too. The longer a projectile stays in flight, the more time air resistance has to act on it and distort its path, so slower, longer-duration flights are generally more susceptible to distortion than fast, short ones.

sections.heading: Vector components of parabolic flight
sections.specBullet: Resolving velocity into horizontal and vertical components

paragraphs: A projectile released at an angle has both upward and forward motion, so its velocity at release can be broken down into two separate vector components. Each is shown as an arrow whose length represents its size.

items.meaning: Represents the forward motion of the projectile. Where air resistance is negligible, as with a shot put, this component stays constant in size throughout the entire flight, because nothing is acting to speed it up or slow it down horizontally.
Represents the upward and downward motion of the projectile. Unlike the horizontal component it is constantly affected by gravity.
The single vector produced by combining the horizontal and vertical components at any instant. It represents the projectile's true direction and speed of travel at that point in its flight.

items: At release, the vertical component is large and positive, moving upward away from the athlete
It shrinks to zero at the peak of the flight, where the projectile is momentarily moving purely horizontally
It then grows increasingly negative as gravity pulls the projectile back down towards landing

sections.heading: Fluid mechanics and dynamic fluid force
sections.specBullet: Fluid mechanics and the two dynamic fluid forces

items.meaning: The study of how an object or the human body moves through a fluid environment, whether a liquid, such as a swimmer moving through water, or a gas, such as a sprinter or ball moving through air.
The two forces acting on a body travelling through air or water: drag, which opposes motion, and lift, which acts perpendicular to the direction of travel.

paragraphs: Both forces influence a wide range of sports, including swimming, cycling, sprinting and any thrown projectile such as a discus or javelin.

sections.heading: Drag: surface and form drag
sections.specBullet: Surface drag and form drag

items.meaning: A resistance force acting in the opposite direction to a body's motion through a fluid, produced by a combination of friction and air or water resistance. It always has a negative effect on velocity.
Also called skin drag. Friction between the outer surface of a moving body and the fluid around it. Elite swimmers shave body hair and wear smooth, close-fitting swimwear specifically to reduce it.
Also called shape drag. Results from the impact of the fluid on the overall shape of a moving body.
Shaping the body to be as thin and straight as possible in the direction of travel, minimising the fluid's resistance. It is how form drag is reduced.

paragraphs: A large form drag on the object at the front of a group also creates a pocket of calmer, less turbulent air or water immediately behind it, which is what makes slipstreaming possible.

sections.heading: Slipstreaming
sections.specBullet: Slipstreaming, or drafting

items.meaning: Also called drafting. Taking advantage of the low-drag pocket of air created directly behind another moving competitor. It is most commonly seen in cycling.

paragraphs: The lead rider meets the air first, and it parts around them rather than reaching the wheel behind. What is left is a pocket of reduced resistance for whoever sits in it. The gap has to stay small, roughly 15 to 30 centimetres off the wheel in front, but held there a following rider spends up to around 30 per cent less energy than they otherwise would.

sections.heading: Factors affecting drag
sections.specBullet: The factors affecting the size of the drag force

items.meaning: The faster a body moves through a fluid, the greater the drag force acting against it. This is why very fast sports such as sprinting, cycling and motor racing place such heavy emphasis on minimising drag through streamlined body positioning.

A larger area facing the direction of travel increases drag, and reducing it lowers drag. Cyclists crouch low over the handlebars rather than sitting upright, and speed skiers adopt a low tucked stance, specifically to reduce it.

A smooth, aerodynamic shape reduces drag. Specialist streamlined equipment and clothing, such as aerodynamic cycling helmets and ridged clothing, streamlined ski helmets extending to the shoulders, and form-fitting suits, are used to gain small, marginal performance advantages.

paragraphs: The opposite case makes the point. An irregular shape with a large surface area relative to its weight, such as a light, feathered badminton shuttlecock, experiences a much larger drag force and loses speed very quickly in flight.

sections.heading: The Bernoulli principle
sections.specBullet: The Bernoulli principle and lift force

items.meaning: Faster-moving air exerts lower pressure, while slower-moving air exerts higher pressure.
A force acting perpendicular to a body's direction of travel, generated by that pressure difference, on projectiles such as the discus.
The tilt of the projectile relative to the oncoming airflow. The amount of lift generated depends on it.

paragraphs: Greater lift keeps a projectile in the air for longer, which increases the horizontal distance it can travel before landing.

sections.heading: Upward lift force: the discus
sections.specBullet: Upward lift force applied to the discus

items: The discus is released with an appropriate angle of attack
Air passing over its curved top surface has a longer distance to travel than the air passing beneath it, so the air above must move faster
Under the Bernoulli principle, that faster-moving air above creates lower pressure, while the slower air underneath creates relatively higher pressure
The higher pressure beneath generates an upward lift force
Time in the air is extended, and the horizontal distance thrown increases

paragraphs: The optimum angle of attack for a discus is generally between 25 and 40 degrees. Too great an angle of attack reduces lift and increases drag instead, causing the discus to stall and lose distance.

sections.heading: Downward lift force
sections.specBullet: Downward lift force applied to skiers, cyclists and racing cars

paragraphs: The same principle can generate a downward lift force, which is useful whenever a performer or vehicle needs to be pressed more firmly into the ground or track to increase friction and grip, rather than lifted into the air.

rows: Formula 1 car

The rear spoiler is angled so air passing over the top of the car travels a shorter, and therefore slower, path than the air passing underneath. That creates higher pressure above and lower pressure below
A downward lift force pushes the car into the track, increasing tyre grip at high speed and through corners
Cyclist
Crouched low over the handlebars, air passing over their back travels a shorter, slower path than the air passing beneath, generating higher pressure above
A downward lift force that helps the tyres grip the road
Speed skier
The same effect generates downward lift
The skis stay firmly in contact with the snow, and the resulting increase in friction helps melt a thin layer of the snow surface, producing a faster, lower-friction surface to ski on
